course: Small Machines & Pharmaceuticals: The Complete Import Business
module_title: Sourcing Machinery from Pakistan, India, and Russia

lessons.title: Pakistan: Millat Tractors and Agricultural Equipment
lessons.body: Millat Tractors is Pakistan's largest tractor manufacturer, producing 20,000 to 25,000 units annually. Their MF-240 and MF-385 models are workhorses for small farms, priced between $12,000 and $18,000 FOB Karachi. For African importers, these tractors suit 20-50 hectare farms. To source directly, contact Millat's export division in Lahore. Request a price list and minimum order quantity (MOQ), typically 5 units for first-time buyers. You'll need an import license, a letter of credit (LC), and a customs broker in your country. Shipping from Karachi to Mombasa takes 20-25 days; to Lagos, 30-35 days. Import duty in Kenya for tractors is 0% (agricultural equipment exemption), but you'll pay 16% VAT. In Nigeria, duty is 5% plus 7.5% VAT. Always inspect before shipping: hire a local agent to check engine hours, hydraulic leaks, and tire condition. Millat offers a 1-year warranty on major components, but you must return faulty parts to Pakistan at your cost. Spare parts are available through Millat's regional distributors in Kenya, Tanzania, and Nigeria. For smaller equipment like wheat threshers or maize shellers, look to Pakistani manufacturers in Faisalabad. Prices range from $2,500 to $7,000. Use Alibaba or Pakistan's Trade Development Authority (TDAP) to find verified suppliers. Always request a pre-shipment inspection certificate from a third party like SGS. Payment terms: 30% deposit, 70% against bill of lading. Avoid full advance payment. For after-sales support, partner with a local mechanic who can service Millat tractors; training is available in Pakistan for $1,500 per person. Start with 2-3 units to test market demand before scaling.

lessons.title: India: Farm Machinery and Small Industrial Equipment
lessons.body: India offers a wide range of affordable farm machinery: Mahindra tractors (20-75 HP), Kubota mini-tractors, and small industrial machines like rice mills and oil expellers. Mahindra's Jivo and Yuvo series start at $8,000 FOB Mumbai. For African conditions, the Mahindra 275 DI (35 HP) is popular in Kenya and Ghana, priced around $11,000. Indian suppliers often quote in INR or USD; always negotiate in USD to avoid currency risk. Minimum order: 1 unit for tractors, but for spare parts, MOQ can be 100 pieces. Import process: obtain an import license, open an LC through your bank (State Bank of India or local bank with correspondent), and arrange shipping from Nhava Sheva or Mundra ports. Transit to Mombasa: 18-22 days. Duty in Kenya: 0% for tractors, 25% for industrial machines. In Tanzania, duty is 10% for tractors. For small industrial equipment like a 500 kg/hr rice mill, price ranges from $5,000 to $15,000. Indian suppliers often provide installation training. Use IndiaMART to find suppliers, but verify with a video call and request factory visit photos. Payment: 30% advance, 70% against copy of BL. Always inspect for rust, missing tools, and correct voltage (Africa uses 220-240V, 50Hz). Spare parts are cheap and available via Indian diaspora shops in Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra. For after-sales, Mahindra has authorized dealers in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa. If not, train a local mechanic using YouTube videos and a service manual. Consider importing a container of mixed machinery to save on freight: a 40ft container from Mumbai to Mombasa costs $2,500-$3,500. Start with a small order of 2 tractors and 1 rice mill to test demand.

lessons.title: Russia: Tractors, Combines, and Municipal Machines
lessons.body: Russia specializes in heavy-duty tractors (Kirovets, Belarus) and combine harvesters (Rostselmash). For African conditions, the Belarus 820 tractor (80 HP) is reliable and simple to repair, priced at $18,000-$22,000 FOB St. Petersburg. Combine harvesters like the Rostselmash RSM 161 start at $150,000, suitable for large farms (200+ hectares). Municipal machines include snow ploughs, street sweepers, and garbage trucks, but these are less relevant for most African importers unless you're in a cold region or municipal contract. Sourcing: contact Russian exporters via the Russian Export Center (REC) or trade fairs like Agrosalon in Moscow. Minimum order: 1 unit for tractors, but combines often require 2+ units. Payment is tricky due to sanctions: use a bank in a neutral country (e.g., UAE or Turkey) or barter trade. Letters of credit from African banks may be rejected; consider advance payment via SWIFT to a non-sanctioned Russian bank. Shipping from St. Petersburg to Mombasa takes 35-45 days. Duty in Kenya: 0% for tractors, 10% for combines. Spare parts are a challenge; order a spare parts kit with your machine (extra $2,000-$5,000). Russian machines are fuel-hungry but durable. For after-sales, few dealers exist in Africa; you'll need to train a local mechanic with a Russian manual (translated). Consider importing used Russian tractors from Ukraine or Belarus instead, as they are cheaper and parts are more available. For municipal machines, check if your local government has a tender; otherwise, skip. Start with one Belarus tractor to test reliability. Always inspect for corrosion and check engine hours. Use a third-party inspection like SGS Russia.

lessons.title: Trade Fairs and Expos in Each Country
lessons.body: Trade fairs are the best way to meet suppliers, see machines in person, and negotiate. In Pakistan, attend the Pakistan Auto Show (Karachi, April) and the Pakistan Agriculture Expo (Lahore, November). Entry is free for trade visitors; bring business cards and a notebook. In India, the top fairs are AgriIntex (Coimbatore, July) and Kisan Mela (Punjab, March). For industrial equipment, attend IMTEX (Bangalore, January). In Russia, Agrosalon (Moscow, October) is the largest agricultural machinery show. Also, attend the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (June) for municipal machines. Before attending, register online and download the exhibitor list. Book meetings in advance with 5-10 target suppliers. At the fair, ask for: price list, MOQ, delivery time, warranty, and spare parts availability. Collect catalogs and take photos of machines. Negotiate on the spot: ask for 5-10% discount for a firm order. Budget $2,000-$3,000 for travel, accommodation, and meals per fair. Many fairs offer free shuttle from major hotels. If you can't travel, use virtual fairs or Alibaba's online trade shows. After the fair, follow up within 48 hours with a summary email. Request samples or a video factory tour. For African importers, some fairs offer subsidies via your local chamber of commerce. For example, the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI) sometimes organizes trade missions. Always verify supplier credentials: check if they are a member of the local chamber or export promotion council. Avoid paying any deposit at the fair; wait until you've done due diligence. Use fairs to compare prices across countries: Pakistani tractors are cheapest, Indian mid-range, Russian most expensive but durable.

lessons.title: Working with Government Trade Agencies
lessons.body: Government trade agencies can help you find verified suppliers, get export documentation, and sometimes access financing. In Pakistan, contact the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP). They provide a list of registered exporters, organize trade missions, and offer market research. In India, the Engineering Export Promotion Council (EEPC) and the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) are useful. For tractors, the EEPC has a directory of Indian tractor exporters. In Russia, the Russian Export Center (REC) offers export insurance, financing, and matchmaking. They have a representative office in Nairobi, Kenya. To work with these agencies, you need to register as an importer. Provide your business license, tax ID, and import history. They will assign a trade officer. Ask for: list of suppliers, price benchmarks, and shipping logistics. Some agencies offer subsidized trade fair participation. For example, REC covers 50% of booth costs for Russian exporters, not importers. But they can connect you. In Africa, your own government's trade ministry can help: Kenya's Ministry of Industrialization, Trade and Enterprise Development has a trade desk. They can issue certificates of origin and help with customs clearance. Also, check for bilateral trade agreements: Pakistan and Kenya have a trade agreement that reduces tariffs. Use this to your advantage. For financing, the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) offers trade finance for imports from these countries. Interest rates are 8-12% per annum. Always get a letter of credit from a reputable bank. Government agencies can also mediate disputes. If a supplier fails to deliver, file a complaint with the agency. Keep all correspondence. Build relationships with trade officers; they can alert you to new suppliers and regulations.

lessons.title: Comparing Quality, Price, and Support
lessons.body: When choosing between Pakistan, India, and Russia, compare on three factors: quality, price, and after-sales support. Quality: Russian tractors (Belarus, Kirovets) are the most durable, built for harsh climates, but have simple electronics. Indian tractors (Mahindra, Kubota) offer good quality with modern features like power steering and oil-immersed brakes. Pakistani tractors (Millat) are basic but reliable, easy to repair with minimal tools. Price: For a 50 HP tractor, Pakistani Millat costs $12,000-$15,000 FOB; Indian Mahindra $13,000-$16,000; Russian Belarus $18,000-$22,000. Add 20-30% for shipping, duty, and clearing. So landed cost in Kenya: Pakistan ~$16,000; India ~$18,000; Russia ~$25,000. For combines, Russian Rostselmash is $150,000 vs Indian $80,000 (but smaller capacity). Support: Indian brands have the best African dealer network (Mahindra in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana; TAFE in Tanzania). Pakistani Millat has limited dealers but spare parts are cheap and available through informal channels. Russian brands have almost no dealers; you must stock spare parts. For small industrial machines, India leads in support with installation and training. Pakistan offers lower prices but you need to arrange your own service. Russia offers the best build quality but highest support burden. Recommendation: For first-time importers, start with Indian tractors for the balance of price, quality, and support. For large-scale farms, Russian combines are worth the investment. For budget-conscious buyers with mechanical skills, Pakistani tractors are a good entry. Always request a spare parts kit (10% of machine value) and a service manual. Negotiate a 1-year warranty. Test the machine before shipping. Consider total cost of ownership over 5 years: fuel, repairs, downtime. Russian machines use more fuel but last longer. Indian machines are fuel-efficient. Pakistani machines are cheapest to repair. Choose based on your farm size, budget, and access to mechanics.
